practiceProblems.title: Line Plots
practiceProblems.description:
Line plots are used to display data points connected by straight line segments.\
They are particularly useful for showing trends over time or continuous data.
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Generate data
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
y = 2*x

# Create the plot
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.title('Line')
plt.xlabel('X-axis')
plt.ylabel('Y-axis')
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
```
How does the code above work?
- Data generation
   - np.linspace(0, 10, 100) creates an array of 100 evenly spaced numbers between 0 and 10
   - y = 2*x creates an array of 100 values for y based on each value of x
- Plot creation
   - plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4)) creates a new figure with a width of 10 inches and a height of 6 inches.
   - plt.plot(x, y) plots the line.
   - plt.title('Line') sets the title of the plot.
   - plt.xlabel('X-axis') and plt.ylabel('Y-axis') label the x and y axes.
   - plt.grid(True) adds a grid to the plot.
   - plt.show() displays the plot.

Go ahead and copy paste the code snippet given above into the IDE and run the code to see the plot.

practiceProblems.description:
Scatter plots display individual data points without connecting lines. \
They are useful for showing the relationship between two variables. \
Check the scatter plot code present in the IDE which creates a scatter plot of random points

practiceProblems.title: Bar charts
practiceProblems.description:
Bar charts are used to represent categorical data with rectangular bars. \
The height of each bar represents the value of the category. Some applications of bar charts are as follows:
- Comparison is Key: Bar charts excel at comparing values across different categories. This makes them ideal for business, social sciences, and many other fields where comparing group performance or characteristics is important.
- Categorical Data: They're best suited for categorical data (like products, regions, demographics) or discrete numerical data that can be grouped into categories.
- Survey Analysis: Bar charts are a go-to choice for visualizing survey results, especially for multiple choice or Likert scale questions.

Check the code given in the IDE - new points to note here are as follows
- Data generation - We have directly created lists instead of creating NumPy arrays
- Plot generation
  - plt.bar(categories, values, color=colors) - This creates the bar chart
     - categories are used for the x-axis positions of the bars
     - values determine the height of each bar
     - color=colors assigns each bar a color from the colors list
  - plt.grid(True, axis='y') - The axis='y' parameter ensures that only horizontal lines are drawn.

- You can assume any population as per your choice. 
- You need to enable only vertical lines.
- You need to generate a horizontal bar chart using plt.barh(countries, population) - here countries becomes the y axis and population is the x axis.

practiceProblems.title: Histograms
practiceProblems.description:
Histograms represent the distribution of numerical data. \
They're particularly useful for understanding the distribution of continuous data.
- Histograms are best for continuous data or discrete data with many possible values.
- They help in understanding the underlying probability distribution of the data.
- The choice of bin size and number can significantly affect the interpretation of a histogram.
- For multimodal distributions, histograms can reveal subpopulations in the data.

Let's create a simple example of a histogram showing the distribution of exam scores. Check out the code in the IDE. Key points about this example:
- It uses a normal distribution to generate mock data, which is common in many real-world scenarios.
- The histogram uses 20 bins to divide the range of scores.
- The y-axis shows the frequency (number of students) in each bin.
- This type of visualization quickly shows the central tendency, spread, and any skewness in the data.

Some new elements in the code for us to learn
- Data generation
  - scores = np.random.normal(70, 10, 1000). 
     - This generates 1000 random numbers following a normal (Gaussian) distribution. 
     - The distribution has a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 10.
     - These numbers represent simulated exam scores for 1000 students.
- Plot generation
  - plt.hist(scores, bins=20, edgecolor='black') - This creates the histogram:
     - scores is the data to be plotted.
     - bins=20 divides the range of scores into 20 equal-width bins.
     - edgecolor='black' sets the color of the edges of each bar to black.
  - alpha=0.75 sets the opacity of the grid lines (0 is fully transparent, 1 is fully opaque)

practiceProblems.title: Customizing Colors and Styles
practiceProblems.description:
Specifying Colors - Colors can be specified in several ways:
- Named colors: 'red', 'blue', 'green', etc.
- Hex codes: '#FF0000' (red), '#00FF00' (green), '#0000FF' (blue)
- RGB tuples: (1, 0, 0) for red, (0, 1, 0) for green, (0, 0, 1) for blue (values from 0 to 1)
- RGBA tuples: Add an alpha value for transparency, e.g., (1, 0, 0, 0.5) for semi-transparent red

Matplotlib supports various line styles:
- Solid: '-'
- Dashed: '--'
- Dotted: ':'
- Dash-dot: '-.'

practiceProblems.title: Stylesheets in Matplotlib
practiceProblems.description:
Style sheets in Matplotlib are pre-defined sets of plot settings that can be applied to change the overall appearance of your visualizations. They provide a convenient way to customize multiple aspects of your plots at once, ensuring consistency across different figures. \
You can view the list of built-in styles using:
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
print(plt.style.available)
```
Some popular built-in styles include:
- 'default': The default Matplotlib style
- 'classic': The classic Matplotlib style
- 'seaborn': A more modern, visually pleasing style
- 'ggplot': Mimics the aesthetics of ggplot in R
- 'bmh': A style inspired by the Bayesian Methods for Hackers book
- 'dark_background': A style with a dark background, useful for presentations

To use a style sheet, you can use the plt.style.use() function. \
We have populated the code in the IDE - go ahead and check it out. You can also change the style sheet to seaborn or ggplot or one of the other variants.

Interestingly - you can also combine styles. Update the code in the IDE with `plt.style.use(['seaborn', 'dark_background'])` and check out the plot.

- fontweight: Weight of the font ('normal', 'bold', 'heavy', 'light', etc.)
- fontstyle: Style of the font ('normal', 'italic', 'oblique')
- fontfamily: Family of the font ('serif', 'sans-serif', 'monospace', etc.)
- color: Color of the text

You can adjust the position of labels by adding padding as well as rotate labels for better readability.

Check out the code in the IDE to see some of the above points in action.

practiceProblems.title: Using Multiple Subplots
practiceProblems.description:
Subplots allow you to create multiple plots within a single figure, which is useful for comparing different datasets or views of the same data.

The most common way to create subplots is using plt.subplots().

You can create a grid of subplots / stack subplots vertically.

Let us understand some key components of the code written in the IDE
- fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6, 4))
   - This creates a figure with 1 row and 2 columns of subplots.
   - figsize=(6, 4) sets the overall figure size to 6 inches wide and 4 inches tall.
   - fig is the Figure object, and axs is an array of Axes objects.
- axs[0].plot(x, np.sin(x)) - This plots the sine function on the first subplot (left).
- axs[0].set_title('Sine') - This sets the title of the first subplot to 'Sine'.
- axs[1].plot(x, np.tan(x)) - This plots the tangent function on the second subplot (right).
- axs[1].set_title('Tangent') - This sets the title of the second subplot to 'Tangent'.
- plt.tight_layout() - This automatically adjusts the spacing between subplots to prevent overlapping.

Update the code in the IDE and create a stack of 4 subplots as per the figure below
- Do not worry about the data - you can populate any 4 charts - the important point here is to try and stack them in a 2x2 stack
- Hint:
   - axs is an array in the code on the right - axs[0] will change to axs[0, 0] and axs[0, 1] for different sections of the subplot

practiceProblems.title: Sharing Axes
practiceProblems.description:
Sharing axes between subplots is useful when you want to align the scales of multiple plots for easier comparison. You can share x-axes, y-axes, or both.

To achieve this, we use sharex and sharey parameters in plt.subplots():
```python
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True)
```

Considerations
- When sharing axes, you typically only need to set labels on one of the shared axes.
- You can still customize individual plots (e.g., different y-axis scales) while sharing the x-axis.

Check out the code in the IDE.

### Task
Create two subplots arranged horizontally. \
In the left subplot, plot y = x^2, and in the right subplot, plot y = x^3. \
Share the y-axis between the two plots. \
Use different colors for each plot.

practiceProblems.title: Pie chart
practiceProblems.description:
Pie charts display data as slices of a circular graph, where each slice represents a category's proportion of the whole.

Run the code in the IDE. This is how the code works
- plt.pie() function - This function creates the pie chart. Here's what each parameter does:
   - sizes: This is a list or array of numerical values that determine the size of each slice in the pie.
   - labels=categories: This assigns labels to each slice. Categories should be a list of strings corresponding to each value in sizes.
   - autopct='%1.1f%%': This adds percentage labels on the slices. %1.1f formats the number to one decimal place. %% adds a percent sign after the number.
   - startangle=90: This rotates the start of the pie by 90 degrees counterclockwise. By default, the first slice starts at the x-axis.
- plt.axis('equal') - This line ensures that the pie chart is drawn as a perfect circle. Without this, the pie might be drawn as an ellipse depending on the plot's aspect ratio.

### Task
Create a pie chart showing the distribution of expenses in a monthly budget (e.g., rent, food, utilities, entertainment). Use the following values
```python
expenses = ['Rent', 'Food', 'Utilities', 'Entertainment']
amounts = [1200, 400, 200, 200]
colors = ['#ff9999', '#66b3ff', '#99ff99', '#ffcc99']
```

practiceProblems.description:
Resampling is the process of changing the frequency of your time series data.
- It can involve either upsampling (increasing frequency) or downsampling (decreasing frequency).
- Common use cases include aggregating high-frequency data to a lower frequency (e.g., hourly to daily) or filling in missing data points in low-frequency data.

Resampling is performed using the resample() function in Pandas for time series data.

Resampling can significantly affect how your data looks when plotted. \
It can reveal trends that might be obscured in high-frequency data.

Run the code given in the IDE. Observe the following
- We created a time series of hourly sales data.
- We then resampled this data to daily and weekly frequencies.
- For each of these, we plotted the sales values over time.

These plots show how the sales values change over time at different granularities, but they don't show the distribution of the sales values themselves.

3D scatter plots display data points in three-dimensional space. \
Each point represents a single data item with three values: x, y, and z coordinates. These plots are useful for visualizing relationships between three variables simultaneously.

- s: Size of the points
- alpha: Transparency of the points
- cmap: Colormap (when color-coding points)
